#### Hideki Shirakawa (1936–2026): the chemist who helped make polymers conduct electricity

*Nature* published a [scientific obituary on 11 November](https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-026-03633-8) for Hideki Shirakawa, who died on **24 August 2026**, aged 90; his death was [announced by the Institute of Science Tokyo on 3 September](https://www.isct.ac.jp/en/news/p9pzp0pmrxls). The date distinction matters: this is a new appraisal of his scientific legacy, not a newly reported death.

Shirakawa developed a method for making coherent polyacetylene films and, with Alan MacDiarmid and Alan Heeger, showed in 1977 that halogen doping could raise their conductivity by about **nine orders of magnitude**, reaching roughly **10^5 S m^−1**. That result overturned the assumption that plastics were necessarily electrical insulators and established conducting polymers as a field spanning polymer chemistry and condensed-matter physics. The three shared the [2000 Nobel Prize in Chemistry](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/chemistry/2000/summary/) for the discovery and development of conducting polymers. The broader legacy includes organic light-emitting devices, photovoltaics, sensors and flexible electronics, although the original doped polyacetylene itself was chemically fragile and did not become the dominant commercial material.

#### AlphaGenome 2 resolves regulatory-variant effects by cell state, but remains a predictive preprint

Google DeepMind released [AlphaGenome 2 and its preprint on 11 November](https://deepmind.google/blog/alphagenome-2-deciphering-how-cells-read-dna-to-better-understand-disease/). The model takes a **1-megabase DNA sequence** plus a tissue, cell type or cell-state condition and predicts gene expression, chromatin accessibility, methylation, contacts, splicing and other molecular readouts. Its cell encoder was trained on more than **100 million single-cell RNA profiles from 68 tissues**; the accompanying resources score about **7 million variants across 510 conditions** and provide enhancer–gene predictions across 640 conditions.

On held-out TenK10K immune-cell benchmarks, AlphaGenome 2 recovered **30%** of 6,346 fine-mapped single-cell eQTLs at **90% precision**, compared with **16%** for a single-cell-fine-tuned AlphaGenome 1 baseline; for GTEx bulk-tissue eQTLs, recall at 90% precision rose from **17% to 26%**. These are retrospective benchmark results from the developers, not experimental discoveries or clinical validation. The authors report that high-precision recall still captures only a minority of causal variants, performance is weaker for inaccessible chromatin, very distal and post-transcriptional mechanisms, and transient, disease and fine neuronal states are underrepresented. Condition embeddings are learned from observational profiles, so they do not establish causal regulatory responses. A [9 November independent preprint](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898/2026.11.06.764851v1) found that AlphaGenome 1 often failed to propagate simulated promoter disruption into downstream RNA-seq predictions; that test does not directly evaluate AlphaGenome 2, but it shows why orthogonal perturbation experiments remain essential.

#### Correcting one UNC13A splice defect restores synaptic function in cellular ALS models

A peer-reviewed, open-access [*Nature* paper published 11 November](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-026-11256-2) tested whether loss of nuclear TDP-43 disrupts synaptic signalling through cryptic splicing of *UNC13A*, a presynaptic vesicle-priming gene. The authors used human iPSC-derived cortical-like neurons and spinal motor neurons, induced TDP-43 loss, deleted the cryptic exon genetically, and developed splice-switching antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs). They also tested splice correction in a mouse engineered with the human *UNC13A* sequence.

Restoring about **30% or more** of normal UNC13A protein was sufficient to recover spontaneous and evoked synaptic transmission in the cell models. The principal electrophysiology comparisons included 19 versus 19 neurons for one ASO/control analysis, 34 control, 30 TDP-43-depleted and 25 ASO-treated spinal motor neurons, and four independent multielectrode-array experiments for network synchrony. Single-synapse release probability moved toward rescue but narrowly missed conventional significance (**P = 0.052**). The mouse experiment established in-vivo splice correction, not improved survival or behaviour. The cultures had homogeneous TDP-43 loss and consisted only of excitatory neurons, whereas human ALS is mosaic and circuit-level effects include inhibitory neurons. This is therefore strong mechanistic and preclinical evidence, not evidence of safety or efficacy in patients.

#### First human safety study of an oral actinide chelator

A [Phase 1, non-randomized trial published in *JAMA* on 11 November](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/article-abstract/2856697) evaluated HOPO 14-1, an oral formulation of 3,4,3-LI(1,2-HOPO) intended to bind internally deposited actinides and some heavy metals. Forty-two healthy adults, six at each of seven dose levels from **100 to 7,500 mg**, received one dose and were followed for 14 days. Recruitment ran from March 2023 to July 2025, with follow-up completed in August 2025 ([NCT05628961](https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05628961)).

No serious adverse events or dose-limiting toxicities occurred. Drug-related events were diarrhea in **31%**, vomiting in **14%**, headache in **12%** and fatigue in **7%**, all mild or moderate; gastrointestinal effects were most evident at the highest doses. Median time to peak plasma concentration ranged from **0.86 to 1.90 hours**, exposure increased with dose, and elimination was mainly fecal with little urinary excretion. The study establishes single-dose pharmacokinetics and short-term tolerability only. It was open-label, single-centre and had no control group; participants were healthy and uncontaminated, so it did not measure actinide removal, repeated-dose safety or clinical benefit after radioactive exposure.

#### A 3.95-billion-year-old gneiss points to transient subduction on the early Earth

A peer-reviewed [*Nature* study published 11 November](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-026-11280-2) reports trondhjemitic gneiss from eastern Hebei, China, dated to **3.95 billion years**. Magmatic zircons have mean **δ^18O = +6.77 ± 0.23‰** and weighted mean **εHf(t) = +1.45 ± 0.27**. Together with whole-rock trace elements, thermodynamic modelling favours **8–16% partial melting** of low-temperature-altered basaltic crust at pressures above **1.6 GPa** and **740–820 °C**—conditions corresponding to burial beyond roughly 50 km.

The authors interpret the cool, rapid burial as a transient subduction event and infer that the basaltic source came from mantle depleted during the Hadean. This adds a rare >3.9-Gyr rock record outside Canada's Acasta complex and supports localized recycling of surface-altered crust by 3.95 Ga. The conclusion is model-dependent and rests on a very sparse surviving rock record; evidence for one transient high-pressure event does not demonstrate globally continuous, modern-style plate tectonics at that time.

#### Halogen-free aqueous electrolyte enables four-electron iodine cycling

A peer-reviewed, open-access [*Nature* paper published 11 November](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-026-11282-0) addresses a central obstacle in aqueous metal–iodine batteries: stabilizing reactive I⁺ intermediates without concentrated, corrosive halide electrolytes. The authors combine a kosmotropic anion, a polar anion and a non-halogen nucleophile. In their mechanism, the polar anion creates a water-poor, anion-rich electrode interface while the kosmotropic anion weakens nucleophile–water interactions, allowing Nuc–I⁺–Nuc halogen bonds to stabilize the four-electron I⁻/I⁰/I⁺ pathway.

The framework worked with four nucleophiles and in Zn–I₂ and Al–I₂ laboratory cells. Zn–I₂ cells retained **96% capacity after 1,000 cycles at 1 A g⁻¹** and **94% after 2,000 cycles at 2 A g⁻¹**, and four-electron conversion persisted up to **12.2 mg cm⁻²** iodine loading. Spectroscopy, micro-CT, molecular simulations and electrochemistry support the proposed interfacial mechanism. Practical readiness remains unproven: most measurements used coin cells, the economic advantage is modelled, and the authors identify incomplete Coulombic efficiency and irreversible iodine-inventory loss that worsens at higher loading. Long-duration pouch-cell validation, safety and system-level energy metrics are still needed.
